title: Does the diagonal sum rule work for the square starting at nine?
description: The expression two a plus eight is tried on a new calendar square whose top left date is nine, and both diagonal sums are found. The board then shows why a few checked squares cannot cover an endless calendar, while the expression with a letter can. Keeko's doubt is that a table of many squares is enough to be sure.
teaching_notes: One idea: checking some squares gives confidence, but only the expression with a letter-number covers every square. Watch for students who think more examples in a table make a proof.

source: Check the expression 2a + 8 on another square whose top left
video_script.why: A learner checks the expression for the diagonal sums on a new square and sees why the letter covers all squares.
video_script.substitution: the book's calendar, with a new square whose top left date is nine
video_script.anchor: the calendar with a square whose top left date is nine
video_script.wrong_answer: checking squares in a table is enough to be sure
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a table of checked squares proves the rule for the whole calendar. The calendar can go on and on, and a square that is not in the table may break the pattern, so only the expression with a letter covers every square.
video_script.payoff_line: Both diagonal sums are twenty six, and the expression covers every square

final_answer.value: 26 for both diagonals when a = 9, and the expression proves it for all squares
final_answer.spoken: both diagonal sums are twenty six, and the expression covers every square

maths_rules: top left a = 9, right is 9 + 1 = 10, below is 9 + 7 = 16, diagonal is 9 + 8 = 17
the calendar has unlimited squares, so checking some squares cannot show all
Keeko test, top left 20: 20 + 28 = 48 and 2 x 20 + 8 = 48 are one more square, still not all squares
video_script.design: The new square with nine at the top left stays on the board. Its dates are written, the diagonals are added, and the result is matched with the expression.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about the calendar.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>The book marks a new square of four dates. Its top left date is nine.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Earlier, the diagonal sums came out as two eigh plus eight. Does this new square agree?

beats.on_screen: the calendar and the new square stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the square with a at the top left; arrows: right is 1 more, below is 7 more, diagonal is 8 more

marks.top: the letter a is written on the top left date
marks.arrows: arrows show 1 more to the right and 7 more below
marks.wk: a week of seven days is written beside the downward arrow

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>In this square, the top left date is the letter eigh.
<bookmark mark='arrows'/>The date to its right is one more. The date below is seven more.
<bookmark mark='wk'/>That is because a week has seven days.

beats.on_screen: Given: top left date a = 9 ; the expression 2a + 8

marks.gv: a = 9 and the expression are written

narration: <bookmark mark='gv'/>Given, the top left date is nine, and the expression is two eigh plus eight.

beats.on_screen: To find: the diagonal sums of this square, and why checking some squares is not enough
narration: <bookmark mark='fd'/>We have to find the diagonal sums of this square. We also say why checking some squares is not enough.
<bookmark mark='right'/>Step one, write the four dates. Nine plus one is ten on the right.
<bookmark mark='below'/>Nine plus seven is sixteen below.
<bookmark mark='diag'/>Nine plus eight is seventeen on the diagonal.
<bookmark mark='d1'/>Step two, add the dates on each diagonal. Nine plus seventeen is twenty six.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>Ten plus sixteen is also twenty six.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 2a + 8 with a = 9 gives 2 × 9 + 8 = 18 + 8 = 26, a match

marks.match: 26 is matched with the diagonal sums

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step three, put nine in place of eigh in two eigh plus eight. Two times nine plus eight is eighteen plus eight.
<bookmark mark='match'/>That is twenty six, which matches both diagonal sums.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: the calendar can go on and on, so there are unlimited squares ; checking some squares cannot show all

marks.endless: the calendar grows beyond 30 with dots
marks.cover: the expression with a is shown covering every square

narration: <bookmark mark='endless'/>Step four, the calendar can go on and on, so there are unlimited squares. We cannot check them all one by one.
<bookmark mark='cover'/>The expression with a letter covers every square at once.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 26 for both diagonals when a = 9 ; the expression proves it for all squares
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Both diagonal sums are twenty six, and the expression covers every square.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the calendar
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: a table of checked squares, struck out; the endless calendar with a square not in the table

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows a table of checked squares
marks.gap: a square outside the table is marked on the endless calendar
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and the expression with a is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks checking squares in a table is enough to be sure.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>But a table holds only the squares we tried. A square that is not in the table may break the pattern.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The expression with eigh works for any top left date, so it covers every square.
